## How Is a Skyscraper Measured?

The question seems simple, but it has divided experts for decades. The **Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH)**, based in Chicago, is the global reference body for skyscraper rankings. It distinguishes three heights for each tower: architectural height (up to the spire or fixed antenna integrated into the design), height to the highest occupiable floor, and height to the absolute top of any antenna.

The official ranking uses **architectural height**. This rule has surprising consequences: One World Trade Center in New York (541 m) outranks the Willis Tower in Chicago (442 m) by including its 124-meter architectural spire, whereas it would fall behind if only occupiable rooftops were measured. The method also distinguishes skyscrapers from other vertical structures: the Eiffel Tower (330 m to the antenna) and the CN Tower in Toronto (553 m) do not appear in the skyscraper rankings, as they do not contain habitable floor space or offices throughout the majority of their height.

This criterion matters. The **Burj Khalifa**, the **Shanghai Tower**, and the **Merdeka 118** are skyscrapers in the fullest sense—they house apartments, hotels, and offices across dozens of floors each. They are not pylons disguised as towers. This is precisely what sets them apart from telecommunication structures that often dominate urban skylines while remaining absent from the rankings.

## The Burj Khalifa (828 m): Dubai's Indestructible Reign

Inaugurated on **January 4, 2010**, the **Burj Khalifa** has now held the top spot in the global rankings for over sixteen years—a record longevity in a field where ambitions follow one another rapidly. With its 828 meters of architectural height, the tower designed by American firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill surpasses the current second-place building by **196 meters**. To visualize that gap: it is approximately the height of the Eiffel Tower from ground to spire.

The construction site mobilized up to **12,000 workers simultaneously**, from over 100 countries. In total, 330,000 m³ of concrete and 55,000 tons of steel were required. To solve the problem of extreme winds at this altitude—which subjected the structure to lateral forces capable of causing oscillations felt by occupants—engineers designed a Y-shaped cross-section at 120°, inspired by the _Hymenocallis_ flower, a plant native to the Arabian desert. This triangular shape breaks up wind vortices and reduces vibrations dramatically.

Construction lasted **six years** (2004–2010), at an estimated cost of $1.5 billion. During the concrete-pouring phases of the upper floors, the structure rose at approximately **one floor every three days**. To pump concrete to over 600 meters of height, engineers developed a high-pressure pumping system that was itself a technical record at the time.

The tower houses **163 habitable floors**, including an Armani Hotel on the first 39 floors, Armani Residences apartments, offices from the 45th to the 108th floor, and two public observation decks: 'At the Top' on the **124th floor** (452 m) and 'At the Top Sky' on the **148th floor** (555 m). From the 124th-floor observation deck, views extend up to **95 kilometers**. On clear days, the Iranian coastline on the far side of the Persian Gulf becomes perceptible on the horizon.

A lesser-known anecdote: during construction, the concrete crews alternated between two slip-forming systems—one for the central core, another for the outer wings—advancing them simultaneously to maintain the structural balance as the building rose. An open-air logistical ballet, managed from control rooms installed right on the floors under construction.

Its nighttime illumination, reprogrammed for special occasions (national holidays, New Year's Eve), is a spectacle visible from dozens of kilometers across the flat desert surrounding Dubai. On some New Year's Eve nights, more than a million people gather at the foot of the tower to watch the fireworks launched from the facade itself.

## The Merdeka 118 (678.9 m): Kuala Lumpur's Giant

![Image 2: Merdeka 118](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_1_3153604a56.jpg)

© Shutterstock

For six years, the **Petronas Towers** (452 m) were the world's tallest skyscrapers between 1998 and 2004, before being surpassed by Taipei 101. Then, at the end of **2023**, Kuala Lumpur completed an even more ambitious tower: the **Merdeka 118** (Jalan Hang Jebat, 50460 Kuala Lumpur, rated 4.6/5 on Google with 2,537 reviews), which rises to **678.9 meters** and now stands as the world's second-tallest skyscraper.

The name "Merdeka" means **"independence"** in Malay. The tower celebrates the 118th anniversary of Malaysia's first cry of independence, proclaimed at the historic gathering of August 31, 1957, in the adjacent Merdeka Stadium—which still exists today, now framed by this monumental tower looming several hundred meters above it.

Designed by Australian firm Fender Katsalidis, the Merdeka 118 draws inspiration from traditional Malaysian Islamic decorative arts. Its facade, composed of **16 triangular facets** that intersect and repeat, reflects the geometric patterns of _mashrabiya_ (arabesque shadow lattices) and the batik fabrics of the region. This is not a generic tower: its architecture tells a cultural identity.

The structure comprises **110 habitable levels** distributed among a Park Hyatt hotel on the lower floors, luxury apartments, offices, and a public observation deck at the top. Construction lasted nearly seven years (2015–2022), the structure was completed at the end of 2023, and the official inauguration took place in January 2024. The total cost exceeds $1.5 billion.

A particular technical challenge: Kuala Lumpur rests on unstable clay layers. The Merdeka 118's foundations plunge **75 meters deep**, with concrete piles reaching the bedrock beneath the alluvial layers. The project required the temporary rerouting of several adjacent traffic lanes throughout the duration of the underground works—a major logistical constraint in such a dense city.

## The Shanghai Tower (632 m): The Spiral That Defies the Wind

In Pudong, Shanghai's financial district, three towers face each other in a striking architectural dialogue: the **Jin Mao Tower** (421 m), the **Shanghai World Financial Center** (492 m, with its rectangular opening at the top nicknamed "the bottle opener" by Shanghainese), and the **Shanghai Tower** (501 Yincheng Middle Road, Pudong, Shanghai, rated 4.6/5 on Google with 3,170 reviews) (632 m), inaugurated in 2015. These three buildings coexist less than 300 meters apart—one of the most spectacular concentrations of skyscrapers in the world.

What sets the Shanghai Tower apart from every other tower in this ranking is its **spiral form**. The tower rotates **120° from base to top**, with a glass outer facade that gradually wraps around itself. This geometry is not decorative: it reduces **lateral wind forces by 24%** compared to a rectangular tower of the same dimensions, generating an estimated savings of $58 million in structural materials. A financially rational decision, dressed up as aesthetics.

The tower is organized into **9 vertical zones** separated by interior atriums that function as suspended micro-neighborhoods: gardens, restaurants, co-working spaces, covered walkways. The concept is that of a vertical city that replicates urban life at 200, 300, and 400 meters of height, rather than cutting its occupants off from it.

The observation deck is located on the **118th floor (546 m)**. The elevators that serve it reach **20.5 meters per second** (73 km/h), covering the distance from the ground floor to the 118th floor in less than **60 seconds**—the fastest in the world when the tower opened.

## The Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower (601 m): The Tower of Mecca

![Image 3: Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_2_7dfff763a3.jpg)

© Shutterstock

The **Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower** (Ajyad Street, Mecca 24231, Saudi Arabia, rated 4.7/5 on Google with 66,665 reviews) is the least known of the top five towers in the global rankings, and certainly the most symbolically charged. Built between 2004 and **2012** in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, it rises to **601 meters** and directly overlooks the Grand Mosque Al-Masjid Al-Haram.

The tower is the central building of a seven-tower hotel complex capable of accommodating more than **100,000 people** simultaneously—a capacity designed to manage the flow of pilgrims during the Hajj, which attracts between 2 and 3 million worshippers each year. With a total floor area of **1.5 million square meters**, it is one of the largest real estate complexes ever built.

The giant clock that crowns the tower has four faces each with a **diameter of 43 meters**—the world's largest clock—lit by 2 million LEDs. At the time of the five daily prayers, the tower lights up in green (the color of Islam) and an Arabic text appears on the clock faces, visible for dozens of kilometers around.

This project was controversial from the outset: construction involved the demolition of an 18th-century Ottoman fortress. Architects and historians protested this heritage loss. The tension between the development of holy cities and the preservation of their history remains intense in academic circles.

## The Ping An Finance Centre (599 m): Shenzhen Against the Sky

![Image 4: Ping An Finance Centre](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_3_df273c1791.jpg)

© Shutterstock

China's fourth-largest city by population, **Shenzhen** was still a fishing village of 30,000 inhabitants in 1979. Four decades later, it has 18 million residents and its skyline rivals those of Dubai or Singapore. The **Ping An Finance Centre** (Fuhua 3rd Road, Futian District, Shenzhen, rated 4.6/5 on Google with 646 reviews), inaugurated in **2017**, is its most visible symbol.

At **599 meters** and 115 floors, the Ping An Finance Centre is the headquarters of Ping An Insurance Group, one of the world's largest insurance companies. The tower was originally designed to reach **660 meters**, but aviation authorities required flashing warning lights above 600 meters—a constraint the developer deemed incompatible with the project's aesthetic. The final height was therefore adjusted during the design phase.

Its reflective glass facade creates a striking effect in overcast weather: the upper portion disappears into the clouds, making the tower impossible to photograph in full from street level. A tower that visually plays with the limits of its own visibility.

## Ranks 6 to 10 in the Global Rankings

![Image 5: gratte-ciel Asie Pacifique](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_4_e32e8b57e2.jpg)

© Shutterstock

The top five towers capture most of the media attention, but ranks 6 to 10 reveal a fascinating geography: the near-total dominance of the Asia-Pacific region and the Arabian Peninsula in the race for height.

**6th: Lotte World Tower (555 m), Seoul, South Korea**

Inaugurated in **2017**, the **Lotte World Tower** dominates the Jamsil district with its 123 floors. Its slender silhouette is inspired by Korean calligraphy brushes and the celadons of the Goryeo era. On the 123rd floor, the 'Seoul Sky' observation deck at **500 meters** features a transparent glass floor allowing visitors to look straight down to the ground below.

The foundations presented an unusual challenge: the Lotte World Adventure amusement park is located directly beneath the building. Engineers designed an isolated foundation system to prevent vibrations from the tower—caused by wind or elevators—from being transmitted to the attractions below. A constraint that had probably never been encountered in the history of skyscraper construction.

**7th: One World Trade Center (541 m), New York, United States**

The **One World Trade Center** is the most symbolically charged skyscraper in this ranking. Built on the site of the September 11, 2001 attacks, inaugurated in **2014** after eight years of construction, it rises to **541 meters**—exactly **1,776 feet**, a deliberate reference to the year of the American Declaration of Independence. This height is no coincidence: it is a date inscribed in concrete and glass, a way of responding to destruction with a symbol. The construction cost reached approximately **$4 billion**.

**8th and 9th: Guangzhou CTF (530 m) and Tianjin CTF (530 m), China**

Tied at **530 meters** each, the **Guangzhou CTF Finance Centre** (2016) and the **Tianjin CTF Finance Centre** (2019) are architecturally twin towers, designed by the same firm Kohn Pedersen Fox for the same developer Chow Tai Fook. The first houses a Ritz-Carlton hotel at the top; the second, a St. Regis with views over the Bohai Sea.

**10th: CITIC Tower (528 m), Beijing, China** (Chaoyang District, Beijing, rated 4/5 on Google with 2 reviews)

The **CITIC Tower**, nicknamed 'China Zun' in reference to a bronze sacrificial vessel from the Shang dynasty (17th–11th century BC), has been the tallest tower in the Chinese capital since its inauguration in **2018**. Its S-shaped form, which genuinely evokes the silhouette of an ancient vase, gives it a rare visual personality in a skyscraper landscape often dominated by rectangular glass facades.

A geographic observation is in order: of these ten towers, **seven are located in China or the Arabian Gulf**. Europe and the Americas each appear with just one tower ([The Shard](https://ryo.co/en/destinations/england/places/view-of-the-shard/)/Varso Tower for Europe, One World Trade Center for the Americas). This is no coincidence—it reflects a decade of economic growth concentrated in these two regions and a desire to materialize that power in concrete.

## The Jeddah Tower: Toward the First Kilometer

![Image 6: Jeddah Tower](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_5_2f75d0c616.jpg)

© Shutterstock

People have been talking about it for years, and its story reads like a great novel: a monumental project, delays, uncertain financing, resumed construction. The **Jeddah Tower** (King Abdulaziz Road, Al Maasarah, Jeddah, rated 4.5/5 on Google with 111 reviews) (formerly known as the Kingdom Tower) should, once completed, become the **first building in history to surpass 1,000 meters**—more precisely **1,007 meters** according to official plans.

Designed by **Adrian Smith**, the architect who had already drawn the Burj Khalifa for Skidmore, Owings & Merrill before founding his own firm Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, the tower was launched in 2013. Construction was halted in 2017, officially due to technical issues related to liquefiable sand layers in the subsoil, requiring a complete overhaul of the foundations. The internal political context in Saudi Arabia—notably the arrest of Prince Al-Waleed bin Talal during the 2017 anti-corruption purge—also weighed on the timeline.

Construction resumed in **2023**, with completion targeted between 2028 and 2030. If this schedule holds, the Burj Khalifa will lose its title after twenty years of reign.

The technical challenges are considerable. At 1,000 meters, wind gusts can exceed **200 km/h**. Atmospheric pressure at the top will be **12%** lower than at the base, requiring adapted pressurization systems for the highest floors. Elevators will need to travel more than 660 meters in single-run cabins—an absolute record for load-bearing cables. And the temperature difference between the ground floor and the top can reach **7°C** on a hot day.

To put these altitudes in perspective: [our Ryo article on the 10 highest mountain peaks in the world](https://ryo.co/en/articles/nepal/katmandou/the-10-highest-peaks-in-the-world/) reminds us that Everest peaks at 8,849 meters—eight times the height of the future Jeddah Tower. Yet building 1,000 meters of steel and concrete in an Arabian desert remains an engineering feat with no equivalent in the history of civil construction.

**Other projects to watch**

The **Dubai Creek Tower** had been announced at 928 meters, but the project has officially been on hold since 2020. In China, a 2021 government directive limited the construction of buildings over 500 meters in mid-sized cities—a reaction to the speculative excesses of the 2010s, which had seen several towers commissioned and then abandoned mid-construction. The next generation of giant skyscrapers will therefore likely be contested between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, with a few selected Asian megacities in their wake. Far from that race, Paris is walked at street level: our From the Mona Lisa to the Notre-Dame Cathedral tour counts 23 stops.

## Europe's Tallest Skyscraper

![Image 7: Gratte-ciel Europe](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_6_d2176b782a.jpg)

© Shutterstock

Europe does not feature in the global top 20 skyscrapers—a fact that often surprises travelers. The reason lies in a combination of factors: listed historic city centers, height restrictions to preserve heritage skylines, an architectural culture that values horizontal density, and real estate markets less inclined toward large-scale vertical speculation than China or the Gulf.

If one adopts the CTBUH geographic scope, which includes Russia within Europe, the title goes to the **Lakhta Center** in Saint Petersburg, the headquarters of Gazprom, with its **462 meters** (118 floors). Inaugurated in **2019**, it dominates the shores of the Gulf of Finland and has profoundly altered the silhouette of a city that had long preserved its neoclassical skyline.

In Moscow, the **Moscow-City** complex groups several towers between 240 and 374 meters. The **Federation Tower East** (374 m, 2017) is its highest point: 95 floors, a white-and-gold glass facade, prestigious offices, and apartments rising above the neighboring skyscrapers.

Within the European Union, it is the **Varso Tower** in Warsaw, inaugurated in **2022**, that holds the record with **310 meters** of architectural height (spire included, 230 m to the rooftop). Designed by British firm Foster + Partners, it houses offices and a hotel.

Until its inauguration, that EU title belonged to **The Shard** in London (309.6 m), designed by Renzo Piano and inaugurated in 2012. Its slender shard-of-glass silhouette has become one of the symbols of the British capital.

In France, the **Tour Montparnasse** (210 m) remains the tallest tower in Paris, despite several proposed new towers at La Défense that never came to fruition. From its observation deck, the 360° view of Paris is rivaled only by the Eiffel Tower—with one advantage: from Montparnasse, the Eiffel Tower itself appears in the panorama. For Antwerp, whose merchants have always claimed a certain grandeur long before the era of skyscrapers, the [Ryo audio guide A Grandeur at the Highest Level](https://ryo.co/en/destinations/belgium/ryocity/antwerp/) recounts how a port city built its reputation over centuries of international trade.

## The Skylines That Changed Everything

![Image 8: skyline urbaine](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_7_8f772b120e.jpg)

© Shutterstock

A single skyscraper does not make a skyline. What is so captivating about great urban silhouettes is the accumulation—the way dozens of towers create an entirely artificial landscape, readable from dozens of kilometers away.

**Hong Kong** is perhaps the world's most spectacular skyline in terms of sheer density. The city has more than **9,000 buildings over 100 meters tall**—more than any other city on Earth. Its silhouette, visible from ships entering Victoria Harbour or from the heights of Kowloon, is composed of hundreds of towers pressed together on a narrow strip of land between mountains and sea. Here, verticality is not a luxury but a geographic necessity.

**Manhattan**, for its part, invented the very concept of the skyline. Its density stems from a geological constraint: the island of New York rests on a solid granite bedrock, ideal for anchoring deep foundations on limited land. Neighborhoods built on less stable ground never experienced the same vertical concentration. The Midtown silhouette—[**Empire State Building**](https://ryo.co/en/destinations/united-states/places/empire-state-building/), Chrysler Building, One World Trade Center—has been reproduced on billions of postcards for a century.

**San Francisco** offers an entirely different lesson in vertical architecture. Constrained by seismic risk (the San Andreas Fault runs through the region), the city did not develop 800-meter towers but a collection of mid-to-high-rise skyscrapers that compose an unmistakable silhouette—Salesforce Tower (260 m), Transamerica Pyramid, 181 Fremont Street. The [Ryo audio guide From Skyscrapers to Fortune Cookies](https://ryo.co/en/destinations/united-states/ryocity/san-francisco/from-skycrapers-to-fortune-cookies/) explores how Chinatown survived the 1906 earthquake while the Financial District burned, and how developers rebuilt higher than ever on uncertain ground.

**Hamburg** offers the opposite lesson: a port city that long resisted verticality, opting instead for horizontal density and the red-brick architecture of its warehouses. The Elbphilharmonie, perched atop a converted cocoa warehouse, or the HafenCity complex show that a great metropolis can leave its mark on history without reaching for the clouds. An urban philosophy that the [Ryo audio guide to Hamburg The Gateway to the World](https://ryo.co/en/destinations/germany/ryocity/hamburg/) documents across 24 audio tracks and 8 kilometers of walking through the port city.

## Observation Decks at the Top of the World

Ascending to the top of a skyscraper means physically understanding the city—perceiving its density, its flows, its geography at a scale impossible from street level. From 400 meters of height, cars become points of light, parks become green patches, rivers become shimmering ribbons.

Here are the main observation decks open to the public in 2026, by height:

**At the Top Sky (555 m), Burj Khalifa, Dubai**

The observation deck on the 148th floor of the Burj Khalifa is the highest glass floor accessible to the public in the world. The VIP package includes a personalized welcome, telescopes, and a cantilevered glass panel from which you look down to the ground 555 meters below. Price: from **300 AED** (approximately €75) for the standard version, up to **500 AED** for VIP. Book **several weeks in advance** between November and March, Dubai's peak season.

**Seoul Sky (500 m), Lotte World Tower, Seoul**

On the 123rd floor of the Lotte World Tower, this observation deck features a transparent glass floor allowing visitors to look straight down 500 meters below. Price: approximately **27,000 KRW** (€18). The sunset, with the meanders of the Han River far below, ranks among the most photographed moments in South Korea.

**Ciel de Paris (196 m), Tour Montparnasse, Paris**

The rooftop terrace of the Tour Montparnasse offers a 360° view with no glass barrier—a decisive advantage for photography compared to other covered platforms. Price: **€20 to €23** depending on the time slot. Open until **11 PM in summer**, making it one of the best spots in Paris for the illuminated city.

**The View from The Shard (244 m), The Shard, London**

The 72nd-floor observation deck is the highest viewpoint accessible to the public in Great Britain. Price: **£28 to £35** depending on the time slot. Beware of London mists: visibility can drop to just a few dozen meters. Morning, before heat haze sets in, is often the best time slot.

**CN Tower EdgeWalk (356 m), Toronto, Canada** (290 Bremner Blvd, Toronto, ON M5V 3L9, rated 4.8/5 on Google with 796 reviews)

Technically a telecommunications tower (outside the skyscraper rankings), the **CN Tower** offers the most adrenaline-fueled observation experience in the world: a walk on the outside of the tower at 356 meters of height, attached only by a harness, on a circular walkway that goes all the way around the structure. Price: approximately **225 CAD** (€150). Advance booking required, weather conditions must be suitable.

A lesser-known but striking alternative: the **Sky Bridge 138** in Kuala Lumpur, the walkway connecting the two Petronas Towers on the 41st and 42nd floors (170 m). Access is free, but spots are limited to **1,800 visitors per day** and are only distributed on the morning itself on-site—arrive at opening time to be sure of getting a ticket.

## Visiting the World's Tallest Towers: What You Need to Know

![Image 9: tours gratte-ciel observation](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_8_9635276164.jpg)

© Shutterstock

A few practical tips to factor in before planning your visit:

**Book in advance.** The Burj Khalifa observation deck sells out up to three weeks ahead during peak season (November–March). The Lotte World Tower fills up within days. Booking online almost always lets you skip queues and get a discounted rate—between 10 and 30% cheaper than at the door.

**Choose your time.** For photography, sunrise (raking light, few crowds) or the evening golden hour (sunset plus the start of nighttime illumination) offer the most interesting conditions. For a pure nighttime view, check opening hours: the Burj Khalifa is open until midnight, the Tour Montparnasse until 11 PM in summer.

**Check the weather.** At 400–500 meters, low cloud cover can reduce visibility to just a few meters. Check the cloud base on a local weather app before heading out. If visibility is forecast below 10 km, consider rescheduling.

**Dress warmly.** Even in Dubai in winter, outdoor platforms at 500 meters expose you to sustained winds. In Seoul in January, temperatures on the platforms can drop well below zero, even if the indoor spaces are heated.

## FAQ

### What Is the Tallest Building in the World in 2026?

In 2026, the tallest building in the world is the **Burj Khalifa** in Dubai, standing at **828 meters** in architectural height. Inaugurated on January 4, 2010, it has held this title for over sixteen years—an exceptional longevity in a field where records change frequently. Second is the **Merdeka 118** in Kuala Lumpur (678.9 m), inaugurated in November 2023. These two towers vastly outpace the rest of the rankings: the third, the Shanghai Tower, stands at 632 meters.

### What Will Be the Future World's Tallest Skyscraper?

The **Jeddah Tower** in Saudi Arabia is the most advanced project aiming to dethrone the Burj Khalifa. Its planned height is **1,007 meters**—the first building to surpass the one-kilometer mark. Construction, halted in 2017 for technical and political reasons, resumed in 2023. Completion is targeted between **2028 and 2030**, with the usual uncertainties surrounding such a monumental project. Architect: Adrian Smith (Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture), who previously designed the Burj Khalifa.

### What Is the Tallest Skyscraper in Europe?

It depends on the geographic scope used. If Russia is included (CTBUH scope): the **Lakhta Center** in Saint Petersburg, at **462 meters**, is the tallest building in Europe (2019). Within the European Union, it is the **Varso Tower** in Warsaw (**310 meters**, 2022). In France, the tallest tower remains the **Tour Montparnasse** in Paris (210 m), despite several proposed new towers at La Défense that never broke ground.

### What Are the 10 Tallest Skyscrapers in the World?

The 2026 rankings by architectural height (CTBUH method):

1.   Burj Khalifa, Dubai, **828 m** (2010)
2.   Merdeka 118, Kuala Lumpur, **678.9 m** (2023)
3.   Shanghai Tower, Shanghai, **632 m** (2015)
4.   Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower, Mecca, **601 m** (2012)
5.   Ping An Finance Centre, Shenzhen, **599 m** (2017)
6.   Lotte World Tower, Seoul, **555 m** (2017)
7.   One World Trade Center, New York, **541 m** (2014)
8.   Guangzhou CTF Finance Centre, Guangzhou, **530 m** (2016)
9.   Tianjin CTF Finance Centre, Tianjin, **530 m** (2019)
10.   CITIC Tower (China Zun), Beijing, **528 m** (2018)

### Can You Visit the Top of the Burj Khalifa?

Yes. The **Burj Khalifa** has two observation decks open to the public: 'At the Top' on the **124th floor** (452 m) and 'At the Top Sky' on the **148th floor** (555 m). Tickets are available online on the official website. Prices range from **€50 to €75** for the 124th floor, up to **€150** for the VIP version on the 148th floor. Advance booking is strongly recommended between November and March. Sunset and sunrise time slots sell out first.

### Is the Eiffel Tower a Skyscraper?

No, not in the strict sense of the term. The **Eiffel Tower** (330 meters to the antenna) is a metal structure with no significant habitable floor space, comparable in concept to the CN Tower in Toronto. According to CTBUH criteria, it does not meet the conditions of a skyscraper, which must contain occupiable floors throughout the vast majority of its height. This is not an architectural criticism—it is simply a matter of definition. If it were included in the skyscraper rankings, it would rank 5th in Europe, behind the Lakhta Center and several towers in Moscow.

## Conclusion

The world's tallest skyscrapers are more than records in a table. They reflect economic, cultural, and political ambitions: Dubai asserting itself on the world stage, Malaysia celebrating its independence by reaching for the summits, China signing its modernity tower by tower, Saudi Arabia aiming for the first kilometer. Every building in this ranking is the product of a political decision as much as an engineer's calculation.

To explore concretely the cities that built these skylines, Ryo's audio guides offer an immersion at street level, into the neighborhoods that grew around these towers, into the stories that conventional guides rarely tell. And for an entirely different perspective on verticality, the [Ryo audio-guided tour of Chamonix, Where the Earth Touches the Sky](https://ryo.co/en/destinations/france/ryocity/chamonix-mont-blanc/) reminds us that the race for height does not belong to architects alone: mountains have been playing the same game for far longer.

## How Is a Skyscraper Measured?

The question seems simple, but it has divided experts for decades. The **Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH)**, based in Chicago, is the global reference body for skyscraper rankings. It distinguishes three heights for each tower: architectural height (up to the spire or fixed antenna integrated into the design), height to the highest occupiable floor, and height to the absolute top of any antenna.

The official ranking uses **architectural height**. This rule has surprising consequences: One World Trade Center in New York (541 m) outranks the Willis Tower in Chicago (442 m) by including its 124-meter architectural spire, whereas it would fall behind if only occupiable rooftops were measured. The method also distinguishes skyscrapers from other vertical structures: the Eiffel Tower (330 m to the antenna) and the CN Tower in Toronto (553 m) do not appear in the skyscraper rankings, as they do not contain habitable floor space or offices throughout the majority of their height.

This criterion matters. The **Burj Khalifa**, the **Shanghai Tower**, and the **Merdeka 118** are skyscrapers in the fullest sense—they house apartments, hotels, and offices across dozens of floors each. They are not pylons disguised as towers. This is precisely what sets them apart from telecommunication structures that often dominate urban skylines while remaining absent from the rankings.

## The Burj Khalifa (828 m): Dubai's Indestructible Reign

Inaugurated on **January 4, 2010**, the **Burj Khalifa** has now held the top spot in the global rankings for over sixteen years—a record longevity in a field where ambitions follow one another rapidly. With its 828 meters of architectural height, the tower designed by American firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill surpasses the current second-place building by **196 meters**. To visualize that gap: it is approximately the height of the Eiffel Tower from ground to spire.

The construction site mobilized up to **12,000 workers simultaneously**, from over 100 countries. In total, 330,000 m³ of concrete and 55,000 tons of steel were required. To solve the problem of extreme winds at this altitude—which subjected the structure to lateral forces capable of causing oscillations felt by occupants—engineers designed a Y-shaped cross-section at 120°, inspired by the _Hymenocallis_ flower, a plant native to the Arabian desert. This triangular shape breaks up wind vortices and reduces vibrations dramatically.

Construction lasted **six years** (2004–2010), at an estimated cost of $1.5 billion. During the concrete-pouring phases of the upper floors, the structure rose at approximately **one floor every three days**. To pump concrete to over 600 meters of height, engineers developed a high-pressure pumping system that was itself a technical record at the time.

The tower houses **163 habitable floors**, including an Armani Hotel on the first 39 floors, Armani Residences apartments, offices from the 45th to the 108th floor, and two public observation decks: 'At the Top' on the **124th floor** (452 m) and 'At the Top Sky' on the **148th floor** (555 m). From the 124th-floor observation deck, views extend up to **95 kilometers**. On clear days, the Iranian coastline on the far side of the Persian Gulf becomes perceptible on the horizon.

A lesser-known anecdote: during construction, the concrete crews alternated between two slip-forming systems—one for the central core, another for the outer wings—advancing them simultaneously to maintain the structural balance as the building rose. An open-air logistical ballet, managed from control rooms installed right on the floors under construction.

Its nighttime illumination, reprogrammed for special occasions (national holidays, New Year's Eve), is a spectacle visible from dozens of kilometers across the flat desert surrounding Dubai. On some New Year's Eve nights, more than a million people gather at the foot of the tower to watch the fireworks launched from the facade itself.

## The Merdeka 118 (678.9 m): Kuala Lumpur's Giant

![Image 2: Merdeka 118](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_1_3153604a56.jpg)

© Shutterstock

For six years, the **Petronas Towers** (452 m) were the world's tallest skyscrapers between 1998 and 2004, before being surpassed by Taipei 101. Then, at the end of **2023**, Kuala Lumpur completed an even more ambitious tower: the **Merdeka 118** (Jalan Hang Jebat, 50460 Kuala Lumpur, rated 4.6/5 on Google with 2,537 reviews), which rises to **678.9 meters** and now stands as the world's second-tallest skyscraper.

The name "Merdeka" means **"independence"** in Malay. The tower celebrates the 118th anniversary of Malaysia's first cry of independence, proclaimed at the historic gathering of August 31, 1957, in the adjacent Merdeka Stadium—which still exists today, now framed by this monumental tower looming several hundred meters above it.

Designed by Australian firm Fender Katsalidis, the Merdeka 118 draws inspiration from traditional Malaysian Islamic decorative arts. Its facade, composed of **16 triangular facets** that intersect and repeat, reflects the geometric patterns of _mashrabiya_ (arabesque shadow lattices) and the batik fabrics of the region. This is not a generic tower: its architecture tells a cultural identity.

The structure comprises **110 habitable levels** distributed among a Park Hyatt hotel on the lower floors, luxury apartments, offices, and a public observation deck at the top. Construction lasted nearly seven years (2015–2022), the structure was completed at the end of 2023, and the official inauguration took place in January 2024. The total cost exceeds $1.5 billion.

A particular technical challenge: Kuala Lumpur rests on unstable clay layers. The Merdeka 118's foundations plunge **75 meters deep**, with concrete piles reaching the bedrock beneath the alluvial layers. The project required the temporary rerouting of several adjacent traffic lanes throughout the duration of the underground works—a major logistical constraint in such a dense city.

## The Shanghai Tower (632 m): The Spiral That Defies the Wind

In Pudong, Shanghai's financial district, three towers face each other in a striking architectural dialogue: the **Jin Mao Tower** (421 m), the **Shanghai World Financial Center** (492 m, with its rectangular opening at the top nicknamed "the bottle opener" by Shanghainese), and the **Shanghai Tower** (501 Yincheng Middle Road, Pudong, Shanghai, rated 4.6/5 on Google with 3,170 reviews) (632 m), inaugurated in 2015. These three buildings coexist less than 300 meters apart—one of the most spectacular concentrations of skyscrapers in the world.

What sets the Shanghai Tower apart from every other tower in this ranking is its **spiral form**. The tower rotates **120° from base to top**, with a glass outer facade that gradually wraps around itself. This geometry is not decorative: it reduces **lateral wind forces by 24%** compared to a rectangular tower of the same dimensions, generating an estimated savings of $58 million in structural materials. A financially rational decision, dressed up as aesthetics.

The tower is organized into **9 vertical zones** separated by interior atriums that function as suspended micro-neighborhoods: gardens, restaurants, co-working spaces, covered walkways. The concept is that of a vertical city that replicates urban life at 200, 300, and 400 meters of height, rather than cutting its occupants off from it.

The observation deck is located on the **118th floor (546 m)**. The elevators that serve it reach **20.5 meters per second** (73 km/h), covering the distance from the ground floor to the 118th floor in less than **60 seconds**—the fastest in the world when the tower opened.

## The Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower (601 m): The Tower of Mecca

![Image 3: Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_2_7dfff763a3.jpg)

© Shutterstock

The **Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower** (Ajyad Street, Mecca 24231, Saudi Arabia, rated 4.7/5 on Google with 66,665 reviews) is the least known of the top five towers in the global rankings, and certainly the most symbolically charged. Built between 2004 and **2012** in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, it rises to **601 meters** and directly overlooks the Grand Mosque Al-Masjid Al-Haram.

The tower is the central building of a seven-tower hotel complex capable of accommodating more than **100,000 people** simultaneously—a capacity designed to manage the flow of pilgrims during the Hajj, which attracts between 2 and 3 million worshippers each year. With a total floor area of **1.5 million square meters**, it is one of the largest real estate complexes ever built.

The giant clock that crowns the tower has four faces each with a **diameter of 43 meters**—the world's largest clock—lit by 2 million LEDs. At the time of the five daily prayers, the tower lights up in green (the color of Islam) and an Arabic text appears on the clock faces, visible for dozens of kilometers around.

This project was controversial from the outset: construction involved the demolition of an 18th-century Ottoman fortress. Architects and historians protested this heritage loss. The tension between the development of holy cities and the preservation of their history remains intense in academic circles.

## The Ping An Finance Centre (599 m): Shenzhen Against the Sky

![Image 4: Ping An Finance Centre](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_3_df273c1791.jpg)

© Shutterstock

China's fourth-largest city by population, **Shenzhen** was still a fishing village of 30,000 inhabitants in 1979. Four decades later, it has 18 million residents and its skyline rivals those of Dubai or Singapore. The **Ping An Finance Centre** (Fuhua 3rd Road, Futian District, Shenzhen, rated 4.6/5 on Google with 646 reviews), inaugurated in **2017**, is its most visible symbol.

At **599 meters** and 115 floors, the Ping An Finance Centre is the headquarters of Ping An Insurance Group, one of the world's largest insurance companies. The tower was originally designed to reach **660 meters**, but aviation authorities required flashing warning lights above 600 meters—a constraint the developer deemed incompatible with the project's aesthetic. The final height was therefore adjusted during the design phase.

Its reflective glass facade creates a striking effect in overcast weather: the upper portion disappears into the clouds, making the tower impossible to photograph in full from street level. A tower that visually plays with the limits of its own visibility.

## Ranks 6 to 10 in the Global Rankings

![Image 5: gratte-ciel Asie Pacifique](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_4_e32e8b57e2.jpg)

© Shutterstock

The top five towers capture most of the media attention, but ranks 6 to 10 reveal a fascinating geography: the near-total dominance of the Asia-Pacific region and the Arabian Peninsula in the race for height.

**6th: Lotte World Tower (555 m), Seoul, South Korea**

Inaugurated in **2017**, the **Lotte World Tower** dominates the Jamsil district with its 123 floors. Its slender silhouette is inspired by Korean calligraphy brushes and the celadons of the Goryeo era. On the 123rd floor, the 'Seoul Sky' observation deck at **500 meters** features a transparent glass floor allowing visitors to look straight down to the ground below.

The foundations presented an unusual challenge: the Lotte World Adventure amusement park is located directly beneath the building. Engineers designed an isolated foundation system to prevent vibrations from the tower—caused by wind or elevators—from being transmitted to the attractions below. A constraint that had probably never been encountered in the history of skyscraper construction.

**7th: One World Trade Center (541 m), New York, United States**

The **One World Trade Center** is the most symbolically charged skyscraper in this ranking. Built on the site of the September 11, 2001 attacks, inaugurated in **2014** after eight years of construction, it rises to **541 meters**—exactly **1,776 feet**, a deliberate reference to the year of the American Declaration of Independence. This height is no coincidence: it is a date inscribed in concrete and glass, a way of responding to destruction with a symbol. The construction cost reached approximately **$4 billion**.

**8th and 9th: Guangzhou CTF (530 m) and Tianjin CTF (530 m), China**

Tied at **530 meters** each, the **Guangzhou CTF Finance Centre** (2016) and the **Tianjin CTF Finance Centre** (2019) are architecturally twin towers, designed by the same firm Kohn Pedersen Fox for the same developer Chow Tai Fook. The first houses a Ritz-Carlton hotel at the top; the second, a St. Regis with views over the Bohai Sea.

**10th: CITIC Tower (528 m), Beijing, China** (Chaoyang District, Beijing, rated 4/5 on Google with 2 reviews)

The **CITIC Tower**, nicknamed 'China Zun' in reference to a bronze sacrificial vessel from the Shang dynasty (17th–11th century BC), has been the tallest tower in the Chinese capital since its inauguration in **2018**. Its S-shaped form, which genuinely evokes the silhouette of an ancient vase, gives it a rare visual personality in a skyscraper landscape often dominated by rectangular glass facades.

A geographic observation is in order: of these ten towers, **seven are located in China or the Arabian Gulf**. Europe and the Americas each appear with just one tower ([The Shard](https://ryo.co/en/destinations/england/places/view-of-the-shard/)/Varso Tower for Europe, One World Trade Center for the Americas). This is no coincidence—it reflects a decade of economic growth concentrated in these two regions and a desire to materialize that power in concrete.

## The Jeddah Tower: Toward the First Kilometer

![Image 6: Jeddah Tower](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_5_2f75d0c616.jpg)

© Shutterstock

People have been talking about it for years, and its story reads like a great novel: a monumental project, delays, uncertain financing, resumed construction. The **Jeddah Tower** (King Abdulaziz Road, Al Maasarah, Jeddah, rated 4.5/5 on Google with 111 reviews) (formerly known as the Kingdom Tower) should, once completed, become the **first building in history to surpass 1,000 meters**—more precisely **1,007 meters** according to official plans.

Designed by **Adrian Smith**, the architect who had already drawn the Burj Khalifa for Skidmore, Owings & Merrill before founding his own firm Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, the tower was launched in 2013. ## How Is a Skyscraper Measured?

The question seems simple, but it has divided experts for decades. The **Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH)**, based in Chicago, is the global reference body for skyscraper rankings. It distinguishes three heights for each tower: architectural height (up to the spire or fixed antenna integrated into the design), height to the highest occupiable floor, and height to the absolute top of any antenna.

The official ranking uses **architectural height**. This rule has surprising consequences: One World Trade Center in New York (541 m) outranks the Willis Tower in Chicago (442 m) by including its 124-meter architectural spire, whereas it would fall behind if only occupiable rooftops were measured. The method also distinguishes skyscrapers from other vertical structures: the Eiffel Tower (330 m to the antenna) and the CN Tower in Toronto (553 m) do not appear in the skyscraper rankings, as they do not contain habitable floor space or offices throughout the majority of their height.

This criterion matters. The **Burj Khalifa**, the **Shanghai Tower**, and the **Merdeka 118** are skyscrapers in the fullest sense—they house apartments, hotels, and offices across dozens of floors each. They are not pylons disguised as towers. This is precisely what sets them apart from telecommunication structures that often dominate urban skylines while remaining absent from the rankings.

## The Burj Khalifa (828 m): Dubai's Indestructible Reign

Inaugurated on **January 4, 2010**, the **Burj Khalifa** has now held the top spot in the global rankings for over sixteen years—a record longevity in a field where ambitions follow one another rapidly. With its 828 meters of architectural height, the tower designed by American firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill surpasses the current second-place building by **196 meters**. To visualize that gap: it is approximately the height of the Eiffel Tower from ground to spire.

The construction site mobilized up to **12,000 workers simultaneously**, from over 100 countries. In total, 330,000 m³ of concrete and 55,000 tons of steel were required. To solve the problem of extreme winds at this altitude—which subjected the structure to lateral forces capable of causing oscillations felt by occupants—engineers designed a Y-shaped cross-section at 120°, inspired by the _Hymenocallis_ flower, a plant native to the Arabian desert. This triangular shape breaks up wind vortices and reduces vibrations dramatically.

Construction lasted **six years** (2004–2010), at an estimated cost of $1.5 billion. During the concrete-pouring phases of the upper floors, the structure rose at approximately **one floor every three days**. To pump concrete to over 600 meters of height, engineers developed a high-pressure pumping system that was itself a technical record at the time.

The tower houses **163 habitable floors**, including an Armani Hotel on the first 39 floors, Armani Residences apartments, offices from the 45th to the 108th floor, and two public observation decks: 'At the Top' on the **124th floor** (452 m) and 'At the Top Sky' on the **148th floor** (555 m). From the 124th-floor observation deck, views extend up to **95 kilometers**. On clear days, the Iranian coastline on the far side of the Persian Gulf becomes perceptible on the horizon.

A lesser-known anecdote: during construction, the concrete crews alternated between two slip-forming systems—one for the central core, another for the outer wings—advancing them simultaneously to maintain the structural balance as the building rose. An open-air logistical ballet, managed from control rooms installed right on the floors under construction.

Its nighttime illumination, reprogrammed for special occasions (national holidays, New Year's Eve), is a spectacle visible from dozens of kilometers across the flat desert surrounding Dubai. On some New Year's Eve nights, more than a million people gather at the foot of the tower to watch the fireworks launched from the facade itself.

## The Merdeka 118 (678.9 m): Kuala Lumpur's Giant

![Image 2: Merdeka 118](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_1_3153604a56.jpg)

© Shutterstock

For six years, the **Petronas Towers** (452 m) were the world's tallest skyscrapers between 1998 and 2004, before being surpassed by Taipei 101. Then, at the end of **2023**, Kuala Lumpur completed an even more ambitious tower: the **Merdeka 118** (Jalan Hang Jebat, 50460 Kuala Lumpur, rated 4.6/5 on Google with 2,537 reviews), which rises to **678.9 meters** and now stands as the world's second-tallest skyscraper.

The name "Merdeka" means **"independence"** in Malay. The tower celebrates the 118th anniversary of Malaysia's first cry of independence, proclaimed at the historic gathering of August 31, 1957, in the adjacent Merdeka Stadium—which still exists today, now framed by this monumental tower looming several hundred meters above it.

Designed by Australian firm Fender Katsalidis, the Merdeka 118 draws inspiration from traditional Malaysian Islamic decorative arts. Its facade, composed of **16 triangular facets** that intersect and repeat, reflects the geometric patterns of _mashrabiya_ (arabesque shadow lattices) and the batik fabrics of the region. This is not a generic tower: its architecture tells a cultural identity.

The structure comprises **110 habitable levels** distributed among a Park Hyatt hotel on the lower floors, luxury apartments, offices, and a public observation deck at the top. Construction lasted nearly seven years (2015–2022), the structure was completed at the end of 2023, and the official inauguration took place in January 2024. The total cost exceeds $1.5 billion.

A particular technical challenge: Kuala Lumpur rests on unstable clay layers. The Merdeka 118's foundations plunge **75 meters deep**, with concrete piles reaching the bedrock beneath the alluvial layers. The project required the temporary rerouting of several adjacent traffic lanes throughout the duration of the underground works—a major logistical constraint in such a dense city.

## The Shanghai Tower (632 m): The Spiral That Defies the Wind

In Pudong, Shanghai's financial district, three towers face each other in a striking architectural dialogue: the **Jin Mao Tower** (421 m), the **Shanghai World Financial Center** (492 m, with its rectangular opening at the top nicknamed "the bottle opener" by Shanghainese), and the **Shanghai Tower** (501 Yincheng Middle Road, Pudong, Shanghai, rated 4.6/5 on Google with 3,170 reviews) (632 m), inaugurated in 2015. These three buildings coexist less than 300 meters apart—one of the most spectacular concentrations of skyscrapers in the world.

What sets the Shanghai Tower apart from every other tower in this ranking is its **spiral form**. The tower rotates **120° from base to top**, with a glass outer facade that gradually wraps around itself. This geometry is not decorative: it reduces **lateral wind forces by 24%** compared to a rectangular tower of the same dimensions, generating an estimated savings of $58 million in structural materials. A financially rational decision, dressed up as aesthetics.

The tower is organized into **9 vertical zones** separated by interior atriums that function as suspended micro-neighborhoods: gardens, restaurants, co-working spaces, covered walkways. The concept is that of a vertical city that replicates urban life at 200, 300, and 400 meters of height, rather than cutting its occupants off from it.

The observation deck is located on the **118th floor (546 m)**. The elevators that serve it reach **20.5 meters per second** (73 km/h), covering the distance from the ground floor to the 118th floor in less than **60 seconds**—the fastest in the world when the tower opened.

## The Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower (601 m): The Tower of Mecca

![Image 3: Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_2_7dfff763a3.jpg)

© Shutterstock

The **Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower** (Ajyad Street, Mecca 24231, Saudi Arabia, rated 4.7/5 on Google with 66,665 reviews) is the least known of the top five towers in the global rankings, and certainly the most symbolically charged. Built between 2004 and **2012** in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, it rises to **601 meters** and directly overlooks the Grand Mosque Al-Masjid Al-Haram.

The tower is the central building of a seven-tower hotel complex capable of accommodating more than **100,000 people** simultaneously—a capacity designed to manage the flow of pilgrims during the Hajj, which attracts between 2 and 3 million worshippers each year. With a total floor area of **1.5 million square meters**, it is one of the largest real estate complexes ever built.

The giant clock that crowns the tower has four faces each with a **diameter of 43 meters**—the world's largest clock—lit by 2 million LEDs. At the time of the five daily prayers, the tower lights up in green (the color of Islam) and an Arabic text appears on the clock faces, visible for dozens of kilometers around.

This project was controversial from the outset: construction involved the demolition of an 18th-century Ottoman fortress. Architects and historians protested this heritage loss. The tension between the development of holy cities and the preservation of their history remains intense in academic circles.

## The Ping An Finance Centre (599 m): Shenzhen Against the Sky

![Image 4: Ping An Finance Centre](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_3_df273c1791.jpg)

© Shutterstock

China's fourth-largest city by population, **Shenzhen** was still a fishing village of 30,000 inhabitants in 1979. Four decades later, it has 18 million residents and its skyline rivals those of Dubai or Singapore. The **Ping An Finance Centre** (Fuhua 3rd Road, Futian District, Shenzhen, rated 4.6/5 on Google with 646 reviews), inaugurated in **2017**, is its most visible symbol.

At **599 meters** and 115 floors, the Ping An Finance Centre is the headquarters of Ping An Insurance Group, one of the world's largest insurance companies. The tower was originally designed to reach **660 meters**, but aviation authorities required flashing warning lights above 600 meters—a constraint the developer deemed incompatible with the project's aesthetic. The final height was therefore adjusted during the design phase.

Its reflective glass facade creates a striking effect in overcast weather: the upper portion disappears into the clouds, making the tower impossible to photograph in full from street level. A tower that visually plays with the limits of its own visibility.

## Ranks 6 to 10 in the Global Rankings

![Image 5: gratte-ciel Asie Pacifique](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_4_e32e8b57e2.jpg)

© Shutterstock

The top five towers capture most of the media attention, but ranks 6 to 10 reveal a fascinating geography: the near-total dominance of the Asia-Pacific region and the Arabian Peninsula in the race for height.

**6th: Lotte World Tower (555 m), Seoul, South Korea**

Inaugurated in **2017**, the **Lotte World Tower** dominates the Jamsil district with its 123 floors. Its slender silhouette is inspired by Korean calligraphy brushes and the celadons of the Goryeo era. On the 123rd floor, the 'Seoul Sky' observation deck at **500 meters** features a transparent glass floor allowing visitors to look straight down to the ground below.

The foundations presented an unusual challenge: the Lotte World Adventure amusement park is located directly beneath the building. Engineers designed an isolated foundation system to prevent vibrations from the tower—caused by wind or elevators—from being transmitted to the attractions below. A constraint that had probably never been encountered in the history of skyscraper construction.

**7th: One World Trade Center (541 m), New York, United States**

The **One World Trade Center** is the most symbolically charged skyscraper in this ranking. Built on the site of the September 11, 2001 attacks, inaugurated in **2014** after eight years of construction, it rises to **541 meters**—exactly **1,776 feet**, a deliberate reference to the year of the American Declaration of Independence. This height is no coincidence: it is a date inscribed in concrete and glass, a way of responding to destruction with a symbol. The construction cost reached approximately **$4 billion**.

**8th and 9th: Guangzhou CTF (530 m) and Tianjin CTF (530 m), China**

Tied at **530 meters** each, the **Guangzhou CTF Finance Centre** (2016) and the **Tianjin CTF Finance Centre** (2019) are architecturally twin towers, designed by the same firm Kohn Pedersen Fox for the same developer Chow Tai Fook. The first houses a Ritz-Carlton hotel at the top; the second, a St. Regis with views over the Bohai Sea.

**10th: CITIC Tower (528 m), Beijing, China** (Chaoyang District, Beijing, rated 4/5 on Google with 2 reviews)

The **CITIC Tower**, nicknamed 'China Zun' in reference to a bronze sacrificial vessel from the Shang dynasty (17th–11th century BC), has been the tallest tower in the Chinese capital since its inauguration in **2018**. Its S-shaped form, which genuinely evokes the silhouette of an ancient vase, gives it a rare visual personality in a skyscraper landscape often dominated by rectangular glass facades.

A geographic observation is in order: of these ten towers, **seven are located in China or the Arabian Gulf**. Europe and the Americas each appear with just one tower ([The Shard](https://ryo.co/en/destinations/england/places/view-of-the-shard/)/Varso Tower for Europe, One World Trade Center for the Americas). This is no coincidence—it reflects a decade of economic growth concentrated in these two regions and a desire to materialize that power in concrete.

## The Jeddah Tower: Toward the First Kilometer

![Image 6: Jeddah Tower](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/ryo-prod-public-398019065442/medium_public_les_plus_haut_gratte_ciel_monde_body_5_2f75d0c616.jpg)

© Shutterstock

People have been talking about it for years, and its story reads like a great novel: a monumental project, delays, uncertain financing, resumed construction. The **Jeddah Tower** (King Abdulaziz Road, Al Maasarah, Jeddah, rated 4.5/5 on Google with 111 reviews) (formerly known as the Kingdom Tower) should, once completed, become the **first building in history to surpass 1,000 meters**—more precisely **1,007 meters** according to official plans.

Designed by **Adrian Smith**, the architect who had already drawn the Burj Khalifa for Skidmore, Owings & Merrill before founding his own firm Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, the tower was launched in 2013. Construction was halted in 2017, officially due to technical issues related to liquefiable sand layers in the subsoil, requiring a complete overhaul of the foundations. AUSTIN (KXAN) — The old saying that everything is bigger in Texas also applies to the state’s skyline as well.

Austin’s recently completed Waterline tower has claimed the title of the tallest building in Texas, ending Houston’s 44-year reign atop the state’s skyscraper rankings. The 74-story tower rises 1,025 feet above downtown Austin, surpassing Houston’s JPMorgan Chase Tower by 23 feet. It is also the 24th-tallest building in the United States.

The milestone marks a new chapter in Texas architecture, which began with the completion of Dallas’ 14-story Praetorian Building in 1909, considered the state’s first skyscraper. More than a century later, Texas is home to some of the tallest buildings in the nation, with Houston, Dallas and Austin all boasting skyscrapers exceeding 875 feet.

### Waterline: Texas’ tallest building

[Waterline](https://waterlineaustin.com/) officially became the tallest building in Texas following its completion in April. Located in downtown Austin, the mixed-use tower stands 1,025 feet tall and contains 74 floors. The project includes hotel, retail and office space, with residential options coming in September.

Beyond setting a state record, Waterline elevated Austin into an elite group of American cities with skyscrapers topping 1,000 feet. That shortlist also includes Atlanta, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, New York City, Philadelphia and San Francisco. Before Waterline’s completion, Houston’s JPMorgan Chase Tower held the Texas height record from 1982 until 2026.

### The 5 tallest buildings in Texas

| Texas Rank | Building | City | Height | Year Completed | U.S. Rank |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Waterline | Austin | 1,025 ft. | 2026 | 24th |
| 2 | JPMorgan Chase Tower | Houston | 1,002 ft. | 1982 | 26th |
| 3 | Wells Fargo Plaza | Houston | 992 ft. | 1983 | 34th |
| 4 | Bank of America Plaza | Dallas | 921 ft. | 1985 | 40th |
| 5 | Williams Tower | Houston | 901 ft. | 1983 | 46th |

### Texas skylines

Texas’ skyscraper history has shifted between Dallas and Houston for much of the last century.

Houston remains the state’s skyscraper capital, holding three of the five tallest buildings in Texas. The aforementioned JPMorgan Chase Tower remains the tallest building in Houston and the tallest pentagonal (five-sided) building in the world.

Dallas’ highest structure, Bank of America Plaza, reaches 921 feet and ranks as the fourth-tallest building in Texas and 40th nationally. Austin, meanwhile, has rapidly climbed the rankings with Waterline and “Sixth and Guadalupe,” which stands 875 feet tall and ranks as the seventh-tallest building in Texas.

[These were Texas’ fastest-growing cities in 2025, according to new Census Bureau estimates](https://www.kxan.com/news/texas/2025-city-population-estimates/)

Today, the state’s tallest towers reflect the economic [growth of its largest cities](https://www.kxan.com/news/texas/2025-city-population-estimates/) and prevalence of the “Texas Triangle,” the nickname of the area where most economic development and [population growth can be found](https://www.kxan.com/news/texas/2025-county-population-estimates/) in Texas.

AUSTIN (KXAN) — The old saying that everything is bigger in Texas also applies to the state’s skyline as well.

Austin’s recently completed Waterline tower has claimed the title of the tallest building in Texas, ending Houston’s 44-year reign atop the state’s skyscraper rankings. The 74-story tower rises 1,025 feet above downtown Austin, surpassing Houston’s JPMorgan Chase Tower by 23 feet. It is also the 24th-tallest building in the United States.

The milestone marks a new chapter in Texas architecture, which began with the completion of Dallas’ 14-story Praetorian Building in 1909, considered the state’s first skyscraper. More than a century later, Texas is home to some of the tallest buildings in the nation, with Houston, Dallas and Austin all boasting skyscrapers exceeding 875 feet.

### Waterline: Texas’ tallest building

[Waterline](https://waterlineaustin.com/) officially became the tallest building in Texas following its completion in April. Located in downtown Austin, the mixed-use tower stands 1,025 feet tall and contains 74 floors. The project includes hotel, retail and office space, with residential options coming in September.

Beyond setting a state record, Waterline elevated Austin into an elite group of American cities with skyscrapers topping 1,000 feet. That shortlist also includes Atlanta, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, New York City, Philadelphia and San Francisco. Before Waterline’s completion, Houston’s JPMorgan Chase Tower held the Texas height record from 1982 until 2026.

AUSTIN (KXAN) — The old saying that everything is bigger in Texas also applies to the state’s skyline as well.

Austin’s recently completed Waterline tower has claimed the title of the tallest building in Texas, ending Houston’s 44-year reign atop the state’s skyscraper rankings. The 74-story tower rises 1,025 feet above downtown Austin, surpassing Houston’s JPMorgan Chase Tower by 23 feet. It is also the 24th-tallest building in the United States.

The milestone marks a new chapter in Texas architecture, which began with the completion of Dallas’ 14-story Praetorian Building in 1909, considered the state’s first skyscraper. More than a century later, Texas is home to some of the tallest buildings in the nation, with Houston, Dallas and Austin all boasting skyscrapers exceeding 875 feet.

### Waterline: Texas’ tallest building

[Waterline](https://waterlineaustin.com/) officially became the tallest building in Texas following its completion in April. Located in downtown Austin, the mixed-use tower stands 1,025 feet tall and contains 74 floors. The project includes hotel, retail and office space, with residential options coming in September.

Beyond setting a state record, Waterline elevated Austin into an elite group of American cities with skyscrapers topping 1,000 feet. That shortlist also includes Atlanta, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, New York City, Philadelphia and San Francisco. Before Waterline’s completion, Houston’s JPMorgan Chase Tower held the Texas height record from 1982 until 2026.

**10th: CITIC Tower (528 m), Beijing, China** (Chaoyang District, Beijing, rated 4/5 on Google with 2 reviews)

The **CITIC Tower**, nicknamed 'China Zun' in reference to a bronze sacrificial vessel from the Shang dynasty (17th–11th century BC), has been the tallest tower in the Chinese capital since its inauguration in **2018**. Its S-shaped form, which genuinely evokes the silhouette of an ancient vase, gives it a rare visual personality in a skyscraper landscape often dominated by rectangular glass facades.

A geographic observation is in order: of these ten towers, **seven are located in China or the Arabian Gulf**. Europe and the Americas each appear with just one tower ([The Shard](link_5)/Varso Tower for Europe, One World Trade Center for the Americas). This is no coincidence—it reflects a decade of economic growth concentrated in these two regions and a desire to materialize that power in concrete.

[](https://cw39.com/news/texas/what-is-the-tallest-building-in-texas-austin-takes-the-crown/)[](https://cw39.com/news/texas/what-is-the-tallest-building-in-texas-austin-takes-the-crown/)[](https://cw39.com/news/texas/what-is-the-tallest-building-in-texas-austin-takes-the-crown/)

The milestone marks a new chapter in Texas architecture, which began with the completion of Dallas’ 14-story Praetorian Building in 1909, considered the state’s first skyscraper. More than a century later, Texas is home to some of the tallest buildings in the nation, with Houston, Dallas and Austin all boasting skyscrapers exceeding 875 feet.

### Waterline: Texas’ tallest building

[Waterline](link_64) officially became the tallest building in Texas following its completion in April. Located in downtown Austin, the mixed-use tower stands 1,025 feet tall and contains 74 floors. The project includes hotel, retail and office space, with residential options coming in September.

Beyond setting a state record, Waterline elevated Austin into an elite group of American cities with skyscrapers topping 1,000 feet. That shortlist also includes Atlanta, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, New York City, Philadelphia and San Francisco. Before Waterline’s completion, Houston’s JPMorgan Chase Tower held the Texas height record from 1982 until 2026.

content:
[Jason M. Barr](https://www.jasonmbarr.com/)April 14, 2026

[Stefan Al](https://www.stefanal.com/)’s latest book is [_Dwelling on Earth: The Past and Future of the Places We Call Home_](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324065739) (Norton, 2026). His previous book was[_Supertall: How the World’s Tallest Buildings Are Reshaping Our Cities and Our Lives_](https://buildingtheskyline.org/stefan-al/) (Norton, 2022). Al earned a Ph.D. in City and Regional Planning from the University of California, Berkeley. He is a practicing architect and has taught at Virginia Tech, Columbia University, Pratt Institute, the University of Hong Kong, and the University of Pennsylvania. He currently teaches in the Urban Policy & Planning Department at Hunter College, City University of New York.

### About the Book

**JB:** Dwelling on Earth _is, roughly speaking, a one-million-year history of human housing and habitation. What inspired you to take such a long-run perspective?_

**SA:** When you take a long view, you find some fascinating parallels between our distant ancestors. Our fundamental building impulse, for instance. We can trace it back to roughly 476,000 years ago at Kalambo Falls in Zambia, where someone fitted two interlocking timbers together—the earliest evidence of a capacity to create a built environment, long before Homo sapiens even existed. From those simple timbers, we have come a long way, via Mesopotamian mud cities and Roman concrete multi-apartment buildings to today’s soaring skyscrapers and sensor-equipped “smart” homes—and possibly soon, 3D-printed moon habitats. But the impulse remains.

### Surprise Findings

**JB:**_In your research for the book, what surprised you the most about housing in the past? What types of housing did you find most intriguing and why?_

**SA:** Of course, dwellings take so many different forms, with variations driven by culture, climate, resource availability, and people’s personal preferences. Nevertheless, one big surprise to me is how many early solutions to dwelling were almost universal, as if we were bound to stumble upon them, because they were common sense. The pit house emerged independently in the Levant, in the Yellow River Valley, in Eastern Europe, and in the Sonoran Desert. Without the masonry skill to erect freestanding walls, societies used the earth itself to provide natural walls. Better still, these semisubterranean structures offered superior insulation, remaining warm in winter and cool in summer.

The other example is that when early settlement communities became better farmers, they virtually all shifted from building circular to rectangular homes—not just in the Near East but across Mesoamerica and Asia. Building rectangular was simply more convenient than round forms to expand homes and cluster them together in a denser settlement.

There are many more examples, from the courtyard house to the street grid—appearing independently in cultures with no contact whatsoever. It’s as though the impulse to build—and the many early forms this took—is part of humanity’s DNA.

![Image 1](https://buildingtheskyline.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Dwelling-on-Earth.jpg)

### Grand Lessons

**JB:**_What do you think are the grand lessons from a long-term view when it comes to both housing and urbanism?_

**SA:** One grand lesson is that housing is never just about shelter—it has broader implications for urbanism, health, social interaction, and the environment that we don’t always consider. In car-centric suburbs, daily walks give way to long commutes, contributing to rising rates of diabetes, heart disease, and obesity. Dense apartment living can limit natural light, affecting mental health—though it can also foster social connection. Even those who live in a house with stairs may live longer, benefiting from the daily cardiovascular exercise. These second-order effects are enormous, and they’re shaped by design choices that seem mundane at the time.

One recurring theme is the continuous struggle with the environment. The specifics vary, but the pattern is consistent. Take ‘Ain Ghazal in the Jordan Valley. About nine thousand years ago, villagers upgraded their homes by plastering floors and mud-brick walls with lime, which made them more water-resistant. But producing lime required wood for burning limestone at extreme temperatures, accelerating deforestation. Trees vanished within a three-kilometer radius. The soil eroded, crop yields shrank, and the village was abandoned.

In Mesopotamia, the same pattern played out at a larger scale—widespread deforestation set off a cascade of salinization and soil degradation that lingered for millennia. The lower stretches of the Euphrates and Tigris, once cloaked in palm and poplar, now lie barren as stretches of desert. In some areas, the soil has become so saline that modern attempts to make sun-dried bricks result in weak bricks that are no longer suitable for construction.

Angkor in Cambodia is perhaps the most dramatic case, and new technology has changed what we know about it. Recent lidar surveys reveal that at its peak in the twelfth century, Angkor sprawled over 350 square miles—dozens of times larger than Rome. What seems like untouched jungle today was once a vast metropolis of dispersed dwellings supported by an elaborate water management system of canals and reservoirs. When climate instability hit, that heavily engineered landscape became its Achilles’ heel. The very complexity that was once its strength made it impossible to maintain as the population declined. These sprawling civilizations proved less adaptable than compact cities like Rome, which—though battered—survived. As today’s megalopolises sprawl ever outward amid accelerating climate change, these fates offer a sobering parallel.

### Dwelling on Earth vs. Supertall

**JB:**_Your previous book,_[Supertall](https://buildingtheskyline.org/stefan-al/)_, was a chronicle of the forces driving the rise of supertall [skyscrapers](https://buildingtheskyline.org/long-live-the-skyscraper/) around the world. What connections do you see across the two books? How does the quest for supertall buildings relate to our quest to find better or novel forms of living, if at all?_

**SA:** In a way, _Dwelling on Earth_ is the prelude to _Supertall_, since it covers much of the story of building prior to the world’s tallest towers today. But both books are animated by the same fundamental questions: what are the ways in which we have shaped our buildings and how did they shape us in return?

There’s a personal connection behind the two books, too. I’ve designed tall buildings as an architect and that was in large part the inspiration for _Supertall_. But as a resident, I’ve lived in strikingly varied homes—a Dutch row house where I cycled safely to school, a communal student residence in Delft with kitchens built for connection, a tiny apartment in Barcelona’s lively old town, a cleverly compact Hong Kong pencil tower, and later to American suburban homes from California to New Jersey. Living in these spaces revealed how deeply they shaped my daily life, relationships, and worldview. That personal journey sparked larger questions about how homes influence our social bonds, our sense of self, and our environmental footprint. I became fascinated by the full arc of human habitation—from the first rock shelters to today’s skyscrapers—and that led to _Dwelling on Earth_.

### **Homes and Cities**

**JB:**_How do you see the connection between home design and urbanism? Which drives which? And what are the key lessons about how we should build homes to foster better, more functional cities?_

**SA:** In the world of archaeology, new discoveries of early “proto cities” are stirring up the debate around the beginning of cities. ​​In these earliest settlements, the home probably drove urbanism. Tell Brak in Mesopotamia, for instance, six thousand years ago, had no sign of monuments such as palaces or temples yet it was larger than a hundred acres.

Households clustered together in neighborhood groups separated by open spaces—each cluster functioning almost like a traditional village but gradually becoming part of something larger. Urbanism there likely emerged from the bottom up, as the organic result of many households pursuing their own interests.

What drove people to create these unprecedented communities in Mesopotamia? One clue lies in a piece of volcanic glass. Obsidian, prized for its ability to be made into sharp tools, was likely the economic engine in Tell Brak. Imported from hundreds of miles away, this precious resource attracted people from far and wide. Each household became a workshop, which contributed to a network of decentralized production and trade. Organizing such exchanges required communication, coordination, and trust—which put these communities on a path toward growing complexity, a path toward urbanism.

### Optimal Home Design

**JB:**_One of the themes of your book is that before we had modern technologies, such as electricity, air conditioning, modern appliances and so on, homes were designed to better fit the environmental conditions in the places they were built. Do you think we should be designing our current homes with climate, weather, and sunlight patterns in mind? And if so, what would be gained by this design approach? Or can we just “power through” environmental conditions using modern technology?_

**SA:** Prior to the industrial revolution, designing with climate was simply common sense. Even Socrates once turned his mind to the ideal home, articulating the essence of passive solar design—a southern overhang that offers comfort in all seasons. The ancient Greeks thought this was so obvious that the playwright Aeschylus mocked anyone who didn’t know it.

Today, though it is often forgotten, design with climate in mind still makes sense, and it doesn’t necessarily cost more. Orientation, geometry, ventilation—these are design decisions, not expensive add-ons. Insulation standards, too, are good examples. In Europe, building codes have long required meaningful standards for insulation and airtightness, and they’ve driven real results without making housing unaffordable.

One example in the US is what I call “obese buildings”—structures so deep and wide that they rely entirely on artificial lighting and cooling, cut off from natural light and air and almost impossible to adapt to new uses. This is a lazy way to build: we just throw energy at the problem instead of utilizing design to solve it.
